questions.q: Which primary haemodynamic mechanism accounts for pulmonary oedema in patients with left-sided congestive heart failure?
options: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure from albuminuria
Primary lymphatic obstruction in the mediastinum
Generalized arteriolar vasoconstriction in the alveoli
questions.explain: Impaired left ventricular emptying causes blood to dam back into the pulmonary veins and capillaries, elevating capillary hydrostatic pressure above plasma oncotic pressure and forcing fluid into alveolar spaces.

open.q: What primary haemodynamic mechanism causes pulmonary oedema in left-sided congestive heart failure?

questions.q: Which plasma protein is the single largest contributor to intravascular colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure?
questions.explain: Albumin accounts for roughly half of total plasma proteins and about 75-80% of plasma colloid osmotic pressure due to its abundance and relatively low molecular weight (~66 kDa).

open.q: Name the plasma protein responsible for generating the majority of intravascular colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure.

questions.q: A 32-year-old Nigerian man presents with massive unilateral non-pitting oedema of his right lower limb and scrotum with thickened, verrucous skin (elephantiasis) caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. What is the underlying mechanism of this oedema?
options: Chronic lymphatic obstruction with interstitial fibrosis
Primary sodium retention by the renal collecting duct
questions.explain: Adult filarial worms (Wuchereria bancrofti) reside in inguinal and pelvic lymphatics, inducing chronic lymphangitis, scarring, and obstruction of lymph drainage (lymphoedema), which causes protein-rich interstitial fluid accumulation and secondary dermal fibrosis.

open.q: What pathophysiological mechanism causes chronic non-pitting lower limb and scrotal oedema (elephantiasis) in lymphatic filariasis?

questions.q: How does reduced effective arterial blood volume in congestive heart failure or hepatic cirrhosis trigger secondary renal sodium and water retention?
options: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation and non-osmotic ADH release
Excess ANP secretion causing sodium retention
Inhibition of renal sympathetic activity and renin release
Direct suppression of aquaporin-2 in collecting ducts
questions.explain: Hypoperfusion of the kidneys stimulates juxtaglomerular renin release, generating angiotensin II and aldosterone (which promotes distal tubular Na+ reabsorption), alongside non-osmotic ADH release that increases free water retention.

open.q: Which neurohumoral hormonal cascade is activated by renal hypoperfusion in heart failure and cirrhosis to drive secondary sodium and water retention?

questions.q: How does active hyperaemia differ fundamentally from passive congestion?
options: Hyperaemia is increased arterial inflow; congestion is impaired venous outflow
Hyperaemia is venous pooling; congestion is arterial inflow
Hyperaemia is always pathological; congestion physiological
questions.explain: Hyperaemia is an active process driven by arteriolar dilation and augmented oxygenated arterial blood delivery (making tissues red), whereas congestion is a passive process caused by impaired venous drainage (accumulating deoxygenated blood and causing cyanosis).

open.q: What is the fundamental haemodynamic difference between active hyperaemia and passive congestion?
accept: Hyperaemia is increased arterial inflow while congestion is impaired venous outflow
Arteriolar dilation versus obstructed venous drainage

questions.q: In chronic passive venous congestion of the lung secondary to mitral stenosis, alveolar macrophages phagocytose extravasated red blood cells and become laden with haemosiderin. What are these cells called?
questions.explain: Elevated pulmonary capillary pressure causes microhaemorrhages into alveoli; alveolar macrophages engulf the red blood cells and degrade haemoglobin into haemosiderin, earning the name heart failure cells.

open.q: Name the haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages classically seen in the lungs in chronic passive venous congestion.

questions.q: At autopsy, the cut surface of a liver from a patient with chronic right-sided heart failure displays mottled red-brown centrilobular zones alternating with pale tan periportal zones. What is the classic descriptive term for this gross appearance?
questions.explain: Chronic passive hepatic congestion causes blood pooling and centrilobular necrosis around the central veins (red-brown) contrasted against better-perfused, often fatty periportal hepatocytes (yellow-tan), resembling a grated nutmeg.

open.q: What descriptive gross pathology term is given to the mottled red-brown and yellow-tan cut surface of a liver with chronic passive venous congestion?
accept: Chronic passive congestion of the liver

questions.q: Minute 1 to 2 mm pinpoint haemorrhages into skin, mucous membranes, or serosal surfaces, typically associated with thrombocytopenia or defective platelet function, are termed what?
questions.explain: Petechiae are 1-2 mm capillary haemorrhages characteristic of low platelet counts or qualitative platelet defects; purpura measures 3-10 mm, and ecchymoses (bruises) are larger than 1-2 cm.

open.q: Name the minute 1 to 2 mm pinpoint haemorrhages into skin or mucous membranes typically caused by thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.

questions.q: Which endothelial-derived molecule mediates initial platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen under high shear stress by binding platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb)?
questions.explain: von Willebrand factor, synthesized by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, acts as a molecular bridge linking subendothelial collagen to platelet surface GpIb-IX-V receptors during primary haemostasis.

open.q: Name the multimeric adhesive glycoprotein that bridges subendothelial collagen to platelet GpIb receptors during primary haemostasis.

questions.q: Platelet aggregation during primary haemostasis depends on conformational activation of which platelet surface integrin receptor that binds fibrinogen bridges between adjacent platelets?
questions.explain: Inside-out signaling triggered by ADP and thromboxane A2 activates platelet GpIIb/IIIa (integrin alpha-IIb beta-3), enabling bivalent fibrinogen molecules to cross-link adjacent platelets into a primary haemostatic plug.

open.q: Name the platelet surface glycoprotein receptor that binds fibrinogen to cross-link adjacent platelets during platelet aggregation.

questions.q: Which membrane-bound glycoprotein expressed on vascular smooth muscle cells and adventitial fibroblasts initiates the extrinsic coagulation cascade upon vascular wall disruption?
questions.explain: Vascular injury exposes extravascular tissue factor (thromboplastin), which complexes with and activates circulating Factor VII to Factor VIIa, triggering rapid thrombin generation in vivo.

open.q: Name the extravascular membrane-bound initiator of the in vivo coagulation cascade that complexes with Factor VII upon vessel injury.

questions.q: How does intact vascular endothelium actively inhibit platelet aggregation and limit clot propagation to the site of injury?
options: By secreting prostacyclin (PGI2) and nitric oxide (NO) and expressing thrombomodulin
By continuously secreting thromboxane A2 and tissue factor into the lumen
By releasing platelet-activating factor and von Willebrand factor into healthy plasma
By expressing high levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 on resting surfaces
questions.explain: Healthy endothelial cells maintain an antithrombotic surface by producing vasodilatory platelet inhibitors (PGI2 and NO), expressing heparin-like molecules that activate antithrombin III, binding thrombin via thrombomodulin to activate protein C, and secreting tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA).

open.q: Name two soluble mediators secreted by intact vascular endothelium that directly inhibit platelet aggregation and cause vasodilation.

questions.q: What are the three primary predisposing factors of Virchow's triad in the pathogenesis of thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, abnormal flow and hypercoagulability
questions.explain: Virchow's triad comprises endothelial injury (dominant in arterial and cardiac thrombosis), stasis or turbulence of blood flow (dominant in venous thrombosis), and hypercoagulability of blood.

open.q: State the three components of Virchow's triad that predispose to thrombosis.
accept: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability
Endothelial damage, stasis or turbulence, and hypercoagulability

questions.q: Grossly and microscopically, ante-mortem thrombi exhibit alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin interspersed with darker layers of trapped erythrocytes. What are these laminations called?
questions.explain: Lines of Zahn are produced by rhythmic deposition of pale platelet-fibrin layers and dark red cell layers in flowing blood, proving that the thrombus formed before death rather than as a post-mortem clot.

open.q: Name the alternating pale platelet-fibrin and dark red-cell laminations that distinguish an ante-mortem thrombus from a post-mortem clot.

questions.q: What is the single most common inherited cause of primary hypercoagulability (thrombophilia) in populations of European descent, caused by a point mutation that renders Factor V resistant to cleavage by activated protein C?
questions.explain: The Factor V Leiden mutation substitutes glutamine for arginine at position 506 (Arg506Gln), eliminating the cleavage site for activated protein C and leading to unopposed thrombin generation.

open.q: Name the most common inherited thrombophilia caused by an Arg506Gln point mutation that makes Factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C.

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with recurrent second-trimester miscarriages, deep vein thrombosis, and a paradoxically prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) that fails to correct on mixing studies. Which acquired prothrombotic condition is most likely?
questions.explain: Antiphospholipid antibodies (such as lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies) interfere with phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays in vitro (prolonging aPTT), while activating platelets, endothelium, and complement in vivo to cause arterial/venous thrombosis and recurrent fetal loss.

open.q: Name the acquired hypercoagulable disorder characterized by arterial or venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, and a paradoxically prolonged aPTT due to lupus anticoagulant.

questions.q: Which four potential fates may a newly formed thrombus undergo over time?
questions.explain: A thrombus may propagate by accumulating more platelets and fibrin, embolize distally, undergo fibrinolytic dissolution (especially when fresh), or become organized by ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts with recanalization of capillary channels.

open.q: List the four possible outcomes (fates) of a thrombus in vivo.
accept: Propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization and recanalization

questions.q: How do arterial thrombi typically differ from venous thrombi in appearance and pathogenesis?
options: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich and pale; venous thrombi are red-cell-rich and dark
Arterial thrombi are red and due to stasis; venous thrombi are pale and atherosclerotic
Arterial thrombi grow toward the heart; venous thrombi against flow
Arterial thrombi occur only in superficial veins
questions.explain: Arterial thrombi form at sites of endothelial injury or turbulence (e.g., ruptured atherosclerotic plaques) under high shear and are firm, grey-white, platelet-rich ('white thrombi'), whereas venous thrombi form in sluggish veins and contain abundant enmeshed red cells ('red/stasis thrombi').

open.q: How do arterial thrombi differ from venous thrombi in gross colour and dominant cellular composition?
accept: Arterial thrombi are pale/grey-white and platelet-rich while venous thrombi are dark red and red-cell-rich
White platelet-rich arterial thrombi versus red erythrocyte-rich venous thrombi

questions.q: Why does disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) paradoxically cause severe widespread bleeding despite being triggered by systemic activation of the coagulation cascade?
options: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors with secondary fibrinolysis
Excess hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors
Absence of endothelial tissue plasminogen activator
questions.explain: Widespread microvascular fibrin thrombosis consumes platelets, fibrinogen, prothrombin, and Factors V and VIII faster than they can be replaced (consumption coagulopathy), while secondary plasmin activation generates fibrin degradation products that further inhibit platelet aggregation and fibrin polymerization.

open.q: Explain why widespread activation of coagulation in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) leads paradoxically to severe haemorrhage.
accept: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors with secondary fibrinolysis
Consumption coagulopathy and secondary activation of fibrinolysis

questions.q: Which laboratory finding reflects cross-linked fibrin breakdown by plasmin and is markedly elevated in both acute DIC and venous thromboembolism?
questions.explain: Plasmin cleavage of Factor XIIIa-cross-linked fibrin polymers generates D-dimers; elevated plasma D-dimer confirms both active thrombin-mediated fibrin cross-linking and secondary fibrinolysis.

open.q: Name the specific fibrin degradation product produced when plasmin cleaves Factor XIIIa-cross-linked fibrin, which is markedly elevated in DIC.

questions.q: What is the anatomical source of over 95% of all clinically significant pulmonary thromboemboli?
options: Deep veins of the lower extremities above the knee
Superficial dorsal veins of the hand
Left atrial appendage in atrial fibrillation
Atherosclerotic plaques of the abdominal aorta
questions.explain: More than 95% of pulmonary emboli originate from deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the large deep veins of the lower limbs (popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins).

open.q: From which anatomical venous network do over 95% of pulmonary thromboemboli originate?
accept: Deep veins of the lower extremities

questions.q: A 64-year-old man collapses and dies suddenly 6 days after pelvic surgery when getting out of bed. Autopsy reveals a large coiled thromboembolus straddling the bifurcation of the main pulmonary trunk. What is the mechanism of sudden death?
options: Acute right ventricular outflow obstruction and electromechanical dissociation
Progressive pulmonary venous hypertension causing chronic cor pulmonale
Massive haemoptysis from bronchial artery erosion
Gradual fibrous obliteration of the alveolar capillaries
questions.explain: A saddle embolus occluding the pulmonary artery bifurcation blocks over 60% of the pulmonary vascular bed, causing abrupt right ventricular pressure overload, acute cor pulmonale, loss of left ventricular preload, and sudden cardiovascular collapse.

open.q: What is the immediate pathophysiological cause of sudden death when a large saddle embolus occludes the pulmonary artery bifurcation?
accept: Acute cor pulmonale and loss of left ventricular preload
Obstruction of pulmonary blood flow causing acute right heart failure

questions.q: How can a venous thrombus originating in the deep veins of the leg cross into the systemic arterial circulation to cause an ischaemic stroke (paradoxical embolism)?
options: An intracardiac right-to-left shunt, commonly a patent foramen ovale
Retrograde flow through the thoracic duct into the aorta
Direct passage from portal veins into the hepatic artery
questions.explain: Paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous embolus bypasses the pulmonary capillary filter by shunting from the right heart to the left heart through an intracardiac communication, most commonly a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect.

open.q: Through what anatomical cardiac pathway does a venous embolus enter the systemic arterial circulation during paradoxical embolism?

questions.q: A 22-year-old motorcyclist sustains a closed mid-shaft femur fracture in a road traffic crash. Forty-eight hours later, he develops sudden tachypnoea, confusion, and a petechial rash over his anterior chest and axillae. Which type of embolism explains this triad?
questions.explain: Fat embolism syndrome classically presents 24 to 72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures with the triad of respiratory insufficiency, neurological symptoms (irritability, delirium, coma), and petechial skin/conjunctival haemorrhages due to mechanical microvessel occlusion and free fatty acid endothelial toxicity.

open.q: Name the syndrome occurring 24 to 72 hours after long-bone fractures characterized by respiratory distress, neurological dysfunction, and upper-body petechiae.

questions.q: Which gas is primarily responsible for forming intravascular bubbles in decompression sickness (caisson disease) when a deep-sea diver ascends too rapidly?
questions.explain: Under high atmospheric pressure underwater, large amounts of inert nitrogen dissolve in blood and lipid-rich tissues; rapid ascent causes nitrogen to come out of solution as gas bubbles that obstruct skeletal muscle vessels ('the bends') and pulmonary capillaries ('the chokes').

open.q: Name the inert gas that comes out of solution as intravascular bubbles during rapid ascent in decompression sickness.

questions.q: During maternal autopsy following sudden collapse and DIC in labour due to amniotic fluid embolism, which characteristic histological finding is identified within maternal pulmonary arterioles and capillaries?
options: Fetal squamous cells, lanugo hair, mucin, and vernix fat
Crystalline cholesterol clefts surrounded by foreign-body giant cells
Calcified psammoma bodies and amyloid fibrils
Gas bubbles surrounded by fibrin-free empty spaces
questions.explain: Amniotic fluid embolism occurs when amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation through torn uterine/cervical veins, depositing fetal squamous epithelial cells, lanugo hair, vernix caseosa fat, and mucin in maternal pulmonary microvessels.

open.q: What fetal-derived microscopic elements found inside maternal pulmonary capillaries confirm the diagnosis of amniotic fluid embolism at autopsy?
accept: Fetal squamous cells, lanugo hair, vernix fat, and mucin

questions.q: Why do infarcts of the lung and small intestine typically appear red (haemorrhagic) rather than pale (anaemic)?
options: Dual blood supply and loose tissue allow blood to enter the necrotic area
Arterial spasm without occlusion is the sole cause
They occur only in avascular tissues
questions.explain: Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur in venous occlusions, loose tissues (such as lung) where blood collects in necrotic alveoli, and organs with dual circulations (lung via bronchial arteries; small intestine via mesenteric arcades) where blood continues to perfuse the devitalized area.

open.q: Why do ischaemic infarcts in the lung and small intestine typically appear red (haemorrhagic) rather than pale?
accept: Dual blood supply and loose tissue allowing blood to enter the necrotic zone
Dual circulation or loose spongy parenchyma

questions.q: Which morphological shape do most arterial infarcts in solid wedge-shaped organs such as the spleen, kidney, and lung assume?
options: A wedge with its apex at the occluded vessel and its base at the organ surface
A spherical lesion centred on the occluded vessel
A linear lesion restricted to the subcapsular cortex
A ring-shaped lesion that always spares the periphery
questions.explain: Because arterial branching radiates outward toward the periphery of solid organs, occlusion produces a pyramidal or wedge-shaped infarct whose apex points toward the focus of vascular occlusion and whose base abuts the serosal surface.

open.q: Describe the characteristic macroscopic shape and orientation of an arterial infarct in solid organs like the spleen or kidney.
accept: Wedge-shaped with apex at the occluded vessel and base at the organ surface

questions.q: Why is the liver relatively resistant to ischaemic infarction compared with the kidney or myocardium?
options: It receives a dual blood supply from both the hepatic artery and the portal vein
Hepatocytes require no oxygen for ATP generation
Its sinusoids lack endothelial cells and basement membranes
It stores sufficient glycogen to sustain anaerobic metabolism for weeks
questions.explain: The liver's dual afferent blood supply—roughly 75% from the portal vein and 25% from the hepatic artery—protects hepatic parenchyma from infarction if only one vessel is occluded (similar to the dual pulmonary/bronchial supply of the lung).

open.q: What anatomical vascular feature makes the liver relatively resistant to ischaemic infarction?
accept: Dual blood supply from the hepatic artery and portal vein

questions.q: Which type of shock is characterized by systemic vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and endothelial activation triggered by microbial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide?
questions.explain: Septic shock is a form of distributive shock driven by dysregulated host inflammatory responses to severe infection (Gram-negative endotoxin, Gram-positive peptidoglycans, fungi), causing widespread nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, microvascular thrombosis, and cellular metabolic dysfunction.

open.q: Name the type of distributive shock caused by dysregulated host immune and vascular responses to severe microbial infection.

questions.q: Which innate immune pattern-recognition receptor on macrophages and endothelial cells binds Gram-negative bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) via CD14 and MD-2 to initiate cytokine storm in septic shock?
questions.explain: TLR4 recognizes Gram-negative bacterial endotoxin (LPS) complexed with LPS-binding protein and CD14, activating NF-kappaB and driving massive secretion of TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and inducible nitric oxide synthase.

open.q: Name the cell-surface Toll-like receptor that recognizes Gram-negative bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to initiate septic shock signaling.

questions.q: During the initial non-progressive (compensated) stage of hypovolaemic shock, which neurohumoral mechanisms maintain perfusion to the heart and brain?
options: Baroreflexes, sympathetic catecholamines, RAAS and ADH
Reduced renin and increased sodium excretion
questions.explain: Early volume loss triggers carotid and aortic baroreceptor firing, increasing sympathetic tone (tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction in skin, gut, and kidneys) alongside RAAS and ADH activation to preserve coronary and cerebral perfusion.

open.q: Which key compensatory neurohumoral mechanisms preserve perfusion to vital organs during the non-progressive stage of hypovolaemic shock?
accept: Baroreceptor reflex, sympathetic activation, RAAS, and ADH
Sympathetic vasoconstriction, tachycardia, and RAAS activation

questions.q: Which severe systemic IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction causes sudden histamine-driven systemic vasodilation, laryngeal oedema, and distributive shock within minutes of allergen exposure?
questions.explain: Anaphylactic shock results from widespread mast cell and basophil degranulation triggered by IgE cross-linking (e.g., penicillin, insect stings, foods), leading to abrupt vascular collapse and bronchospasm.

open.q: Name the acute distributive shock state caused by systemic IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and massive histamine release.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman survives prolonged haemorrhagic shock after a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, but develops oliguria with muddy brown granular casts in her urine 48 hours later. Which renal lesion is the most characteristic morphological manifestation of shock?
questions.explain: Renal cortical vasoconstriction and hypoperfusion during shock cause ischaemic injury and sloughing of proximal and thick ascending limb tubular epithelial cells—acute tubular necrosis—producing oliguria and pigmented granular casts.

open.q: Name the characteristic renal parenchymal lesion caused by prolonged hypoperfusion in shock that presents with oliguria and muddy brown granular casts.

questions.q: At autopsy of a patient who died of septic shock, the lungs are heavy, firm, and red, and histology demonstrates diffuse alveolar damage with pink proteinaceous membranes lining the alveolar ducts. What are these intra-alveolar structures called?
questions.explain: Shock lung (acute respiratory distress syndrome, ARDS) features diffuse alveolar epithelial and capillary endothelial injury with leakage of protein-rich oedema fluid and necrotic cell debris that form glassy eosinophilic hyaline membranes lining alveoli.

open.q: Name the glassy eosinophilic proteinaceous linings found inside alveoli in shock lung (acute respiratory distress syndrome).
